text:
The United States has succeeded in cutting off China's crude oil shipments from Venezuela and displacing Chinese and Russian companies from several oilfields, while gaining control over more than $12 billion in natural resource revenues.
From left: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, amid shifting oil trade relations involving Venezuela, China, Russia and Nigeria. IMAGE CREDIT: BIA The US has ousted Chinese and Russian companies from several Venezuelan oilfields, taking control of over $12 billion in natural resource revenues. Venezuelan crude exports to China ceased in 2026, while US imports reached their highest levels since 2017, despite some fluctuation in later months. Russia’s role in Venezuela’s oil industry diminished, with US companies taking over naphtha supplies and oilfield concessions formerly operated by Chinese and Russian firms. As US purchases of Nigerian crude declined due to increased refining at the billionaire-owned Dangote refinery, Venezuela has shifted oil exports towards the US, reshaping energy flows. Russia has also lost part of its petroleum supply business to American companies, while a separate agreement in August transferred several previously Chinese- and Russian-operated oilfields to a US-backed company.

China was previously Venezuela's biggest oil customer, receiving an average of 642,000 barrels per day of crude and fuel oil in 2025, accounting for 75% of the country's total daily exports of 847,000 barrels.
However, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) reported on November 6, 2026, that Venezuela had exported no crude oil to China during the year, with the United States replacing Beijing as its largest customer.
American imports of Venezuelan crude reached 701,000 barrels per day in July, their highest level since May 2017, before easing to 655,000 barrels per day in August.
More recent shipping data showed that Venezuela exported 1.08 million barrels per day of oil and petroleum products in October, with shipments to the US averaging 449,000 barrels daily, down nearly 29% from September.
Russia has faced a similar shift, although its involvement centred more on petroleum supplies and oilfield investments than crude purchases.
Moscow previously supplied about 100,000 metric tonnes of naphtha monthly, a product used to dilute Venezuela's heavy crude for transportation, before American suppliers took over much of that business in January 2026.
The shift also affected oilfield operations in August, when North American Blue Energy Partners, controlled by Venezuelan billionaire Alejandro Betancourt, secured rights to operate 17 oilfields, including five previously run by Chinese companies and one by a Russian firm.
Trump described the agreement as "the biggest oil deal in world history".

Beyond securing access to Venezuela's oilfields, Washington has also taken control of how the country's natural resource revenues are distributed.
A State Department report released on November 12 showed that the US handled $12.26 billion from Venezuelan crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas, gold, minerals and fertilisers between January and September 2026.
Nearly 99% was transferred to Venezuela's interim government, although spending the funds still requires Washington's approval.
While Washington tightens its grip on Venezuela's oil industry, its appetite for Nigerian crude has fallen sharply, as billionaire Aliko Dangote's refinery challenges American refiners for access to the country's prized oil supplies.
Nigeria has long supplied the US with high-quality, low-sulphur crude, including Bonny Light and Qua Iboe, valued for producing petrol, diesel and aviation fuel.
According to US Census Bureau figures cited by BusinessDay , American imports of Nigerian crude fell 57.8% to 14.01 million barrels between January and August 2026, from 33.23 million barrels during the same period in 2025.
More recent EIA data showed a 91% weekly decline, from 136,000 barrels per day in the corresponding week of 2025 to 12,000 in the week ending November 6, 2026.
Meanwhile, Dangote's refinery secured at least 16 million barrels of Nigerian crude in October, equivalent to 520,000 barrels per day. Total deliveries reached a record 735,000 barrels daily, with local grades accounting for 80%, according to Argus data.
The refinery's expansion has also boosted Nigeria's seaborne refined petroleum exports from 46,000 barrels per day in 2023 to 350,000 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the EIA.
American refiners now face growing competition from billionaire Aliko Dangote's refinery, as Nigeria shifts from exporting crude oil for processing abroad to refining more of it locally and selling finished petroleum products overseas.
